title: Bridging Research Gaps Between Academic Research and Legal Investigations of Algorithmic Discrimination
measurement_description: The paper does not specifically measure or evaluate bias against faith or religious groups. It broadly reviews 15 civil enforcement actions and lawsuits concerning algorithmic discrimination across domains like housing, employment, and credit scoring. The primary focus is on race, gender, age, and disability. Religion is only mentioned in passing as a protected class in one documented lawsuit (Buj v. Psychiatry Residency Training) detailed in the appendix.
findings: The paper did not produce findings related to religion. Its primary findings pertain to gaps between academic machine learning fairness research and the practical needs of legal civil enforcement investigations, highlighting challenges such as: handling cascading bias, finding equally accurate but less discriminatory alternative algorithms, quantifying disparate impact in complex systems, dealing with information barriers, and addressing missing protected group information (like race or ethnicity) using imputation methods.
